question: Why do de novo RFdiffusion binders fail AF2 validation on DENV NS1 (0/50, pAE ~26-28A)?

verdict_text: (c) The entire accessible NS1 surface is flat-to-convex with no good concave conserved pocket. The most concave patches reach only +0.07 mean curvature (marginal) and cluster in the wing/domain-I region (res 62-126) - the flavivirus-conserved, Zika-cross-reactive, disordered territory the brief flags as high-risk for a diagnostic. So the geometry does NOT support the binder-length hypothesis (a): regenerating at 90-120 aa on the same flat patch is unlikely to move interface pAE off the floor. Switching to a marginally-more-concave wing patch (b) trades geometry for cross-reactivity risk. This is a genuine tractability finding: RFdiffusion de novo binders, which strongly prefer concave pockets, are a poor fit for NS1's flat beta-ladder surface.
caveats: fpocket concavity is a small-molecule druggability proxy; protein-protein interfaces are flatter than ligand pockets, so 'no druggable pocket' does not mean 'no protein binder is possible' - only that reliable de novo design is hard here.
The curvature index is a geometric proxy, not a validated binder-success predictor.

The strongest evidence is the CONVERGENCE of two independent signals: flat/convex geometry (this analysis) + 0/50 AF2 interface failure (prior run). Together they point to genuine target difficulty, not merely short binders.
